## 1. Canonical Definitions & Standing Rules

### Why This Book Exists — The Dictionary Problem

A major premise of the entire book — and the reason it is called *"What Is Love?"* — is that the deeper Patrick studies apologetics, the more he sees that **Christians disagree not because they disagree on Scripture, but because they disagree on what words mean.** Catholics and Protestants are often reading the same verses but carrying different dictionaries. The most important word to define is **love**. Once that definition is settled — with its four pillars intact — most of the other disagreements (faith/works, grace/merit, sacraments, authority) begin to fall into place. The book is, at bottom, a dictionary entry for the most important word in the Christian vocabulary.

### The Canonical Definition of Love

> **"God's Perfect Love is the sacred gift of covenant which binds truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice into life-giving communion."**

Word-for-word, no variation. Note: without "sacrificial" — Patrick's deliberate choice. The four pillars (Truth, Justice, Mercy, Sacrifice) are co-constitutive. **No pillar is metaphysically prior to any other.**

### The Aquinas Integration (Patrick's Key Insight)

> **"In Augustine's definition of love being willing the good of the other, I think the good in that definition is the truth, justice and mercy. And the willing it for the other is the sacrifice part."**

`amor est velle alicui bonum` — **the good** (bonum) = Truth + Justice + Mercy; **willing it for another** (velle alicui) = Sacrifice. The four pillars are not four additions to the definition — they are its interior anatomy.

Cross-test: Calvary = Aquinas at full volume. *Bonum* = truth about our condition + justice satisfied + mercy poured; *velle alicui* = "for us men and for our salvation" at the cost of everything.

### Standing Rules (Never Violate)

- **RSV translation required** for all Scripture quotations
- **Matt 28 must always include v.18** (Christ's authority) — never just 28:19-20
- **Never use:** `performed`, `earned`, `transaction`, `payment plan`, `debt-payment`, `unmercy`, `destiny` (banned everywhere in the book, 2026-10-29, except inside verbatim quotes), `imputed` / `imputation`
- **`checklist` is permitted** when naming the reduction we warn against — i.e., love minimized into a checklist of items stripped of its underlying obligations of truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice. Do not use it to describe authentic love itself.
- **Use only Catholic sources for theological authority** — do not cite or quote Protestant thinkers as authorities. Frame all doctrinal support through Catholic voices (Scripture, the Catechism, the saints, Catholic thinkers). Secular sources (e.g., social science, history) may be cited as corroboration, not as theological authority — e.g., Jonathan Haidt in Ch. 15.
- **Never frame Protestant traditions or figures polemically or defensively** — always positive, charitable framing. Naming a Protestant tradition or individual is acceptable when the reference is respectful (e.g., citing a Protestant author approvingly).
- **Pillar interplay goes in Binding Check only** — don't cross-pollinate pillar arguments in body sections
- **OT sacrifices "spoke truly of" fulfillment** — never "merely foreshadowed" or diminished
- **"Sacrifice completes"** is acceptable; **"sacrifice carries the others"** is NOT (implies priority)
- **No Oxford comma in the canonical pillar list:** "truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice"
- **Facets, one image only (Patrick, 2026-10-07):** every part of the definition (sacred, gift of covenant, binding, truth, justice, mercy, sacrifice, life-giving communion) is a *facet* of one love, like one diamond seen from every side. Truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice are facets too, never a separate class with a title of their own; when the four are meant, name them (“truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice”); when the whole is meant, say “the facets of love.” Avoid “the four facets,” which suggests love has only four. Never “pillars” or “threads.” Do not stretch the diamond image (cutting, carbon bonds) unless absolutely necessary. Said of God, the four are not four things but one with His being (todo 61). Supersedes the 2026-09-29 “pillars” rule and the 2026-10-06 “four marks” ruling. Book-wide rework: Future Task 167.
- **Prefer prose over bullets** — convert bullet lists to flowing narrative paragraphs
- **Gender-neutral language** where applicable (e.g., "the person" not "he" for generic references)
- **Each example must be placed under the correct pillar** — a pundit's hypocrisy is truth-without-sacrifice, not truth-without-justice; use the framework precisely

### Writing Guidelines (added 2026-10-29, from the Cowork session review)

Guidelines for writing new content and for double-checking important concepts. They do not log edits already made.

**Words and wording**

- **Avoid "progressive".** Use "progression" or another word.
- **Never change a quote from an outside source.** No rule in this file alters a quotation from Scripture, the Catechism, a Church document, or any other source. A quote stays verbatim, even when it contains a banned or discouraged word.
- **"Grace" is a loaded word.** In each chapter, use "Perfect Love" wording at least once in your own words where the passage is for general readers: "God's Perfect Love", "Jesus' Perfect Love", "the Lord's Perfect Love" or "His Perfect Love". Not every instance must change. Technical terms such as "the law of grace" may stay.
- **Never write that God forces His gifts on us.** Do not write "makes us righteous"; write "formed", "conformed" or "transformed". Jesus does not "master" us: we kneel and give ourselves to Him.
- **Do not call a same-sex union a "marriage".** Name the ideal "Complementary Covenant Marriage".
- **Never say a source teaches more than it does.** Check each claim of the form "exactly what the Church teaches".
- **Virtue names are human words for larger truths.** Never write that the book "defines" them. Offer the virtue matrix humbly, as leanings for the reader to consider, not as dogma.

**Voice and plain language**

- **Write plain English.** Spell out "churchy" phrases and textbook definitions in concrete, everyday words, or define them in the sentence.
- **Be concise.** Add the smallest text that works. No "word salad", and nothing "wordy and heady".
- **Do not dramatize.** Prefer a plain statement to a flourish.
- **Be humble when offering a test or proof.** Write "one way to test this is…", not an assertion.
- **Do not end sections with a formula** such as "if you have read this far". Vary the closing refrain.
- **Do not re-argue covered ground.** Assume the reader already accepts that faith alone is dead. Make no polemic against "faith alone"; make only the positive case that faith works through love.

**Concepts to get right**

- **Faith** is an ascent/submission of the mind and will (or heart and soul, or heart, mind and soul), never intellectual assent alone.
- **Truth, justice and mercy are the core principles.** Sacrifice makes them real. Sacrifice without the other three is not actuated love.
- **Humility** comes with or before faith. It is the submission of the whole self to God. True humility includes sacrifice.
- **The fear of the Lord** is the beginning of wisdom. It is loving God and neighbor. It becomes concrete through named virtues, including hatred of sin. It is a lifelong journey, never instant.
- **Cooperation with God** is total gift, like spouses who each give everything.
- **Atheists** have the natural law written on their hearts. They can take part in God's truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice, but imperfectly and without justification. Atheism lacks the ability for true temporal or eternal communion. Communion needs united hearts, minds and souls and agreed truth.
- **Never say God created us "for incorruption".** God created us VERY GOOD.
- **Men and women.** Men generally lean toward Justice and women toward Mercy. State as fact that sex is ordered to the creation of children and the unity of spouses. The same-sex counterfeit idolizes emotional bonding without a sacrificial desire for covenant.

**Working rules for Claude**

- **Redlines.** Show every proposed edit as a rendered redline: removed text in red strikethrough, added text in green. Use colored text only. Never use a white background or any fill. It must read well in dark mode. Show the full text. Wait for `y` or `n`. Never show a git diff.
- **After Patrick approves one redline, go straight to the next.** Ask one issue at a time. "Skip" or "good as is" means leave it and move on.
- **Link every file or chapter you mention**, so Patrick can open it. After multi-file edits, give one link per file.
- **Move finished items** from "In Progress" to "Completed" in this file without asking.
- **When you report todos,** print the exact todo text first, then your comment.
- **Log only new rules for the whole book.** Do not record individual chapter edits here. Record a decision only when it sets a new rule for the entire book, and give the reason (why, not only what).
- **Stay in scope.** Log off-topic findings as a todo. Do not fix them. A kickoff prompt for a new session says "stay on topic", omits unrelated or already-flagged items, points to existing files instead of restating them, and carries no content from the previous chapter.
- **Read-aloud review method.** Read the whole chapter first. Rate each finding HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW or NOTE. Give the exact line, a quote, and a before and after. Never propose cutting load-bearing doctrine or Scripture for length. Write a styled HTML report in `chapters/reports/` with a summary table. Make no edits. Then walk through the findings one at a time.

## 2. Patrick's Voice & Style

### How Patrick Writes & Edits

- **Concrete over abstract** — when a proposed phrase is too conceptual, he'll say it outright: *"just a whole bunch of words that don't have much meaning."*
- **Favors parallel grammatical structures** — tracks asymmetries closely (notices "two clauses with 'giving,' two without").
- **Thinks theologically by talking through it** — long voice-dictated paragraphs reveal his reasoning; then asks the AI to capture and compress what he just said.
- **Things said once, in the right place** — frequently asks "is this already covered elsewhere?" before adding content.
- **Steelmans opponents without naming them** — repeatedly insists on positive Catholic framing without polemical posture.
- **Tight syllogisms over extended arguments** — prefers a sharp 3-sentence sequence over a paragraph of explanation.
- **Uses "vibe" / "feel" language first** to describe what he wants a passage to convey emotionally, then gets into content specifics.
- **Short approvals for drafts** — "y", "b", "option a" — reviews entire proposed drafts, then simply confirms or adjusts.
- **Catches his own imprecision** — "But wait, is that example truth without justice?" — will push back on his own edits when the theology drifts.
- **"I'm not asking you to add these exact words... I just want the theology to be deeply felt."**

### Signature Phrases & Motifs Patrick Returns To

1.  **"The open hand / closed fist"** — central controlling metaphor for sacrifice; can be extended, even temporarily broken, but must return to it
2.  **"Our love is never oriented inward. It's always oriented outward."** — personal conviction from his conversion
3.  **"We sacrifice because He first sacrificed"** — echo of 1 John 4:19 grammar
4.  **"Faith leads to love. Love grows faith. Round and round."** — spiral image of sanctification
5.  **"A future filled with good Catholics"** — his missional vision
6.  **"His perfect love is what saves the world"** — chapter-close thesis phrase
7.  **"To love is to be someone who sacrificially wills the truth, justice, and mercy of God for another"** — working definition, recited with reader at key moments
8.  **"The only difference is the preposition"** — refers to the theological distinction "not *alongside* but *into*" (our sacrifice united *into* Christ's one sacrifice, not running parallel to it); the italicized preposition carries the whole theological weight
9.  **"As we forgive"** — Our Father clause, returned to repeatedly as the practical binding of mercy and sacrifice
10. **Augustine's restless heart** — *Confessions* 1.1.1, reached for multiple times
11. **Irenaeus "man fully alive"** — *Against Heresies* 4.20.7, brought up unprompted twice

## 3. Theological Positions Settled

### On Faith and Works (The Positive Case)

- **Gal 5:6** as central anchor: "faith working through love" — not faith *plus* love, not faith *and then* love — one organic reality
- **"Faith working through love is faith sacrificing for the other"** — Patrick's own formulation
- **Phil 2:12-13** as synthesis verse: "work out your own salvation... for God is at work in you" — we work out because God is at work
- The spiral: *"Faith leads us to love. Love grows us in faith. Round and round — not as a treadmill, but as the very spiral of life itself"*
- **Never defensive against Protestant readings** — never set up and rebut; simply state the fullness
- Steelman the Protestant concern: *"they are guarding something precious — that what saves us is what Christ did, not what we do"*
- But: **rejected "finished work" language** — *"I don't want to give ground on his finished work because I think they have a completely wrong interpretation of that"*
- Revised steelman: *"our hope rests on His Cross, not on our offerings"*

### James 2 — Patrick's Outward-Facing Reading

> **"I've been thinking about these verses for years... every Protestant argues this from the standpoint of what this verse is saying about me and my salvation. But what James is pointing out here is what I have been saying since I came back to the Catholic faith, that our love is never oriented inward. It's always oriented outward."**

The question is not *"am I really saved?"* — it is *"did anyone get fed? The brother is still hungry."*

James 2:14-17 unpacked as a four-pillars X-ray: "Be warmed and filled" without action fails on all four at once — not seeing (truth), not giving what's owed (justice), heart unmoved (mercy), no cost paid (sacrifice).

### On Sacrifice: Co-constitutive, Not Primary

- **"No thread is metaphysically prior"** — AGENTS.md §4 rule, repeatedly honored
- Found and fixed: "carries the other three into actual effect" → *"makes truth, justice, and mercy actual rather than admired from a safe distance"*
- The closed-fist posture is the **prior reality** from which none of the four pillars can operate — neutral on will-vs-intellect debate (lets Thomists and Augustinians both read correctly)
- **"We do not sacrifice alongside His one sacrifice but into it"** — the preposition *into* is load-bearing

### On Divine Mercy / Universal Offer

- The offer is universal (no sin beyond reach, CCC 605)
- Reception is free (the free "yes" preserved)
- NOT universalism — explicitly: *"for the soul who freely turns and asks for it"*
- God will never abandon us; but love, to be love, leaves us free to abandon Him
- Three outcomes when mercy is extended: acceptance, rejection, **or enablement** (mercy that avoids accountability is not mercy)
- Assurance is real — we can have assurance that God will always hold up His end; we trust Him. We just don't trust ourselves to hold up ours. *"The assurance of a beloved who stays, not the guarantee of a contract I can't break."*

### On *Incurvatus in Se* & the Closed Fist

Augustine's term for the soul curved in on itself. Patrick linked it directly to the closed-fist metaphor: *"The closed fist is incurvatus in se made visible."* Sacrifice liberates from this prison of self.

The seven deadly sins analysis: NOT primarily a refusal of sacrifice (Patrick checked this). The right framing is the closed-fist posture as the prior reality from which none of the four pillars can operate.

### On the Book's Hidden Thesis

> **"Only a church that finds its origin in God as love does, and is willing to look at the fullness of truth in all of God's revelation as love does, and is willing to define what justice requires... is the church that has actually preserved the fullness of love that Christ has taught."**

Submission to the Magisterium = submission to God's love (not to a human institution). No sin is ever merely personal — every sin is ecclesial and cosmic.

### On the Church: Divine Institution, Not "Inspiration" (2026-10-14)

Patrick's conviction: God is the author of the Church. Christ founded her, instituted the Chair of St. Peter, gave the keys and the power to bind and loose, baptize and forgive, and sent her out with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matt 28:18–20). To submit our intellect and will to Christ is to submit them to His Church, and there is nowhere else to go (John 6:68).

**Rule:** never call the Church, Tradition or the Magisterium "divinely inspired" or *theopneustos*. In Church usage, inspiration means God is the author of a text (Dei Verbum 11). Every use of "inspired" in Dei Verbum refers to Scripture. Vatican I states that the Spirit was promised to Peter's successors "not so that they might, by his revelation, make known some new doctrine, but that, by his assistance, they might religiously guard and faithfully expound" the deposit (*Pastor Aeternus* 4). Dei Filius ch. 2: Scripture is sacred not because the Church approved it, but because God is its author.

**Use instead:** the Church, Peter's chair and the sacraments are of *divine institution* ("by the institution of Christ himself," *Pastor Aeternus* 2); the Spirit is her soul (CCC 797); Tradition, Scripture and the Magisterium work together "under the action of the one Holy Spirit" (DV 10) and "flow from the same divine wellspring" (DV 9); the Pope is guided by the Spirit's *assistance*. Christ's own founding acts are more than inspired: they are God the Son acting in person.

**Corollaries:** (1) The Church is holy because she is Christ's own, sanctified and joined to Him (CCC 823). "Perfect" means everything He wills her to be, not sinless members. (2) Trust is in Christ's chair, not the man in it. A pope can err in non-definitive teaching (Honorius I, John XXII) without the Church failing. Indefectibility means she is never bound to error definitively. (3) A Catholic who thinks something is wrong may and sometimes must make his case from within (Gal 2:11; can. 212 §3), but may never leave. Schism = "the refusal of submission to the Roman Pontiff or of communion with the members of the Church subject to him" (CCC 2089).

## 15. Apologetics Approach

### Protestant Engagement Rules

- **Never name Protestant traditions directly.**
- **Always steelman the concern** they are guarding: *"our hope rests on His Cross, not on our offerings."*
- **State the Catholic positive case** so thoroughly it "trounces the faith-alone half-truth" without ever naming it.
- **Matt 28:18** — always include v.18 (Christ's authority); note who is in the room (the eleven Apostles, not a generalized crowd).
- The spiral of faith and love: *"Faith leads us to love. Love grows us in faith."* Not faith *plus* works. One organic reality.

### Patrick's Catholic Salvation Sequence

> **He loves us first → we come to trust Him in faith → in that trust we learn His ways of love → and we obediently live them out in sacrificial love.**

No boasting, no earning. Every step is grace. But precisely because it's a living relationship: *"Every single day I can choose to stop listening."*
